strengths: First asymptotic analysis of attention in the extensive-rank regime; derives sharp learning curves, thresholds, and spectral laws with exact asymptotics
Exceptional quantitative agreement between theoretical predictions and Adam simulations (Figures 1-3) across broad range of sample complexities despite non-convexity
Rigorously formalizes how weight decay induces nuclear-norm regularization on attention matrices, clarifying implicit bias toward low-rank solutions
Cleanly isolates inductive bias of factorized vs. non-factorized parameterization through theoretical comparison and experiments
Reproduces key empirical phenomena observed in transformers: low-rank structure, separated spectral outliers as samples increase
Methodologically solid: extends AMP theory to multi-token softmax setting with non-separable priors; combines GMT and AMP in novel way
Excellent reproducibility: code provided, extensive appendices with detailed derivations, computational implementation details specified
Honestly acknowledges model simplifications and their implications; clear about scope and limitations
weaknesses: Proof presented as 'Claim' with acknowledged 'proof sketch' rather than complete theorem; key steps incomplete: (i) Gaussian universality for multiple tokens relies on extending [48,41,28] without full details, (ii) replicon condition (Eq. 10) only empirically verified ('AMP converged in experiments'), not analytically proven—this condition is crucial for establishing AMP tightness in non-convex setting yet lacks rigorous validation

Substantial gap between model and practical transformers limits relevance: tied (not separate Q,K,V) attention, single head (not multi-head), Gaussian i.i.d. token inputs (not structured text embeddings), fixed T=O(1) sequences, supervised tasks on synthetic data (not self-supervised pretraining on natural data), identity value matrix

Cannot explain all empirically observed phenomena in real networks: MP target reproduces low-rank structure and outliers but fails to capture power-law tails; authors acknowledge this but defer exploration to future work

Limited technical novelty in proof techniques: predominantly adapts existing frameworks (AMP [38,39,51], Gaussian universality [41,28,48], GMT [49,50], spin-glass methods [33,34,35]); extension to multiple tokens and softmax is useful but incremental

Replicon condition (Eq. 10) not analytically verified; complex expression involving ReLU and second derivatives; relying on post-hoc convergence of AMP algorithm as validation is backwards reasoning and limits confidence in theoretical guarantees

Algorithmic insights limited: characterizes global minima but not optimization dynamics; does not explain why non-convex attention loss is trainable by gradient descent—acknowledged as 'challenging problem for future work'

Finite-dimension behavior not characterized: no analysis of minimal d for asymptotic validity, convergence rates, or finite-d effect scaling; simulations use d=100-200 but asymptotic regime not explicitly confirmed
Main empirical validation uses narrow hyperparameter range (λ=0.01, β=β₀=1, Δ=0.5, T=2); limited systematic exploration of sensitivity across parameter space

strengths: Novel application of AMP and random matrix theory to attention learning; the reduction to matrix sensing and state evolution analysis is technically sophisticated
Rigorous characterization of implicit bias from weight decay as nuclear-norm regularization; clean comparison isolating inductive advantage of factorization
Sharp asymptotic results with exact formulas for learning curves and spectral distributions (Eq. 13); strong quantitative agreement with Adam simulations
Spectral predictions (bulk splitting, outlier separation) qualitatively align with empirical observations in real transformers
Thorough mathematical development with extensive appendices providing complete state evolution equations and detailed derivations
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Main result (Claim 1) is presented as unproven claim with only proof sketch. Key steps missing: (1) Gaussian universality extension from T=1 to T>1 is non-trivial but unjustified; (2) Replicon condition (Eq. 10) is required for convergence but unproven—only empirically verified in experiments

Replicon condition is unverified technical assumption essential for theoretical guarantees. Authors acknowledge direct evaluation is 'numerically demanding' and provide no proof or principled verification method—this is circular reasoning using AMP convergence to validate replicon assumption

Severe gap between model and practice: single-head tied attention with Gaussian inputs, fixed sequence length T=O(1), structured bilinear targets vs. real multi-head untied transformers with natural data and variable sequences

Limited practical relevance: does not explain power-law tails in real transformers (acknowledged as future work); validated only on synthetic tasks at small scale (d=100-200); no experiments on actual transformer weights; generalization to multi-head/untied settings unclear
Incomplete proofs with unsubstantiated claims of universality beyond Gaussians; reliance on cited universality results without self-contained arguments about applicability to this specific setting
Gradient descent analysis left incomplete (finds global minima empirically but labeled as 'highly non-trivial phenomenon' for future work); numerical solution of Eq. (7) not clearly explained

Limited experimental validation: factorized vs. non-factorized comparison only on synthetic data; spectral predictions not quantitatively validated on real transformers; claims about echoing 'empirical trends' are qualitative

strengths: Novel and technically sophisticated extension of AMP/spin-glass methods to non-convex attention problems, moving beyond prior Bayes-optimal analyses to characterize ERM solutions
Strong experimental validation with quantitative agreement between asymptotic theory predictions and Adam optimization across multiple regimes (Figures 1-2), non-trivial for non-convex settings

Multiple significant theoretical insights: (1) rigorous characterization of implicit nuclear-norm regularization from weight decay inducing low-rank structure, (2) exact interpolation/recovery thresholds with closed-form expressions, (3) spectral law prediction matching empirically observed phenomena
Compelling demonstration that factorized parameterization substantially outperforms non-factorized (Frobenius) regularization with quantified O(κ₀⁻¹) gap in recovery thresholds (Figure 3, Appendix D)

Honest and thorough presentation of model limitations with clear positioning as foundational theory analogous to Gaussian multi-index models; extensive appendices with complete state evolution and AMP algorithms support reproducibility
Elegant theoretical framework reducing tied attention to generalized matrix sensing with nuclear-norm regularization, unifying the analysis across sequence-to-sequence and sequence-to-label tasks
weaknesses: Main technical result (Claim 1) presented as sketch of proof rather than complete proof; key steps including Gaussian universality extension to multiple tokens and AMP upper/lower bound generalizations explicitly deferred to future work despite authors acknowledging substantial additional work needed

Replicon condition (Eq. 10) required for AMP convergence and tightness is verified only empirically (Adam reaching same optima as AMP) rather than theoretically; authors acknowledge general proof is 'difficult' and direct evaluation 'numerically demanding', leaving a gap in theoretical guarantees for non-convex setting

Substantial gap to realistic transformers: model assumes single-head with tied key/query and identity values (vs. multi-head untied projections), Gaussian synthetic inputs (vs. natural data), fixed sequence length T=O(1) typically T≤5 (vs. variable long sequences), and does not reproduce power-law spectral tails observed empirically

Quadratic sample complexity n = O(d²) required by model does not match practice; while justified by model degrees of freedom, this significantly limits predictive power for understanding actual transformer learning dynamics

Limited empirical scope: experiments only at d=100-200 dimensions with Gaussian synthetic data; no exploration on natural datasets or scaling to realistic dimensions; small scale limits validation of asymptotic predictions

Technical presentation density: Claim 1 with six order parameters and implicit definitions difficult to parse; mapping to vector weights model (B.2) adds complexity; practical implications of theoretical insights for understanding real transformers not clearly articulated

strengths: Novel theoretical framework providing first high-dimensional asymptotic analysis linking spectral properties to generalization in attention layers
Rigorous mathematical development combining random matrix theory, spin-glass theory, and approximate message passing in an integrated framework
Comprehensive experimental validation showing excellent agreement between theory and gradient descent across multiple regimes
Interpretable error decomposition (overfitting, underfitting, approximation, mismatch terms) that connects spectral structure to generalization
Qualitative predictions of empirical phenomena in real transformers (low-rank structure, spectral outliers, power-law scaling)
Honest and thorough discussion of model limitations and assumptions
Practical insights about factorized vs non-factorized parameterization and inductive biases of weight decay
Clear presentation with informative figures and extensive reproducible details in appendix
weaknesses: Main results formulated as 'Claims' rather than theorems; complete proofs require substantial additional technical development, and replicon condition verified only numerically
Conjecture E.1 (extension beyond strict scaling regime) is crucial for Section 4 and 5 results but lacks rigorous proof despite strong numerical support
Highly simplified model with restrictive assumptions: tied attention, single head, synthetic attention-indexed tasks, Gaussian data, finite T=O(1)
Large gap between theoretical model and practical transformers; predictions only validated on synthetic data, not real transformers or datasets
Limited mechanistic justification for why factorization outperforms despite reduced expressivity; nuclear norm connection deserves more prominence
Computational cost (60,000 CPU hours) and complexity of state evolution equations may limit reproducibility
Theoretical framework does not address multi-head attention, which is standard in practice
Power-law scaling laws derived for specific target structure; unclear if mechanism applies to realistic data distributions
